summary:
Belgium prohibits discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics. Same-sex marriage and adoption are legal, and legal name and gender-marker change rests on self-determination.

Under the Law of 25 June 2017, in force since 1 January 2018, transgender people change their registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, with no medical conditions attached. The Federal Justice Department records that the Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019 and that, pending replacement provisions, applications continue to be handled under the existing procedure.

The official Brussels-Capital Region guidance on changing the sex marker on an identity card still lists a medical certificate attesting to a sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision, among the requirements. That application is free of charge, takes three to six weeks, and is made in person at the commune, with a digital mode available.

Minors face a separate track: those aged 12 to 16 may change first name only, while 16 and 17-year-olds may apply for a sex change with parental consent plus a psychological opinion confirming that the decision is freely made.

Hate crime and hate speech on grounds of gender identity are criminal offences, but an international hate-crime monitoring framework records that Belgian legislation does not define hate crimes and provides no code to record them as such; violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions instead.

Equality bodies report rising violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people despite the country's progressive reputation, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases handled by the equality body Unia in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is dating-app traps: victims lured through fake profiles to isolated meetings, then ambushed, beaten, robbed or humiliated. A case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went before Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025, and police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported because of fear or shame.

Conversion practices were banned on 20 July 2023, with penalties of eight days to two years' imprisonment and fines of 208 to 2400 euros. Europe's first femicide law, adopted in 2023, covers all gender-based homicide.

Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, although a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for nonconsensual interventions.

Same-sex couples have held equal adoption rights since 2006 and lesbian couples can access IVF. Since 1 January 2015 a mother's female partner is recognised as co-mother without an adoption procedure, ending an inequality that had required one while the husband of a biological mother was automatically recognised as father.

The 2017 law was framed by the Justice Minister, Koen Geens, as placing self-determination at the centre: a purely administrative procedure with all medical conditions, including sterilisation and surgery, scrapped, alongside a reflection period and public-order safeguards.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map country page sets out Belgium's formal-law position across legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality and non-discrimination, family, civil society, asylum and intersex categories, providing the standard comparative index snapshot of the framework.

Travel industry guides describe Belgium as one of the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers, pointing to a thriving queer culture in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège. That reputation sits alongside the documented rise in violence reported by equality bodies and police.

The Ihsane Jarfi case marks the enforcement ceiling: on 22 December 2014 a Liège court jury convicted four people of the homophobic murder, the first Belgian crime officially qualified as hate-motivated on sexual-orientation grounds. A 2019 study found that 90% of LGBT people in Brussels had suffered verbal or psychological harassment, and a human rights body reported 125 homophobic discrimination cases in May 2018, including 17 physical attacks and 42 public insults.

State hostility is essentially absent at the level of major institutions, but right-wing political hostility has existed. The Flemish Block/Vlaams Belang and the National Front voted against same-sex marriage; Flemish Interest later softened its stance, with its leader stating in 2015 that the party would not campaign to repeal same-sex marriage and its chairman condemning an MP who criticised same-sex marriage and adoption in 2019. N-VA was criticised for joining a European parliamentary group containing homophobic parties.

Sex between men was decriminalised as far back as 1795 under the French penal code, though public-indecency laws and police harassment persisted afterwards. Age of consent has been equal at 16 regardless of sexual orientation since 1795, with a period from 1965 to 1985 when article 372bis set it at 18 for same-sex acts; that provision was repealed on 18 June 1985.
localsOnly:
The Institute for the Equality of Women and Men published 'Being transgender in Belgium - Ten years later' in 2017, a large survey study covering gender identity, coming out, openness, obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed per experienced gender, official name and gender registration change, work, sex work, economic status and well-being.

Justice Minister Koen Geens reported in May 2017 that name-change requests rose from 85 in 2012 to 187 in 2016.

In 2019, Flemish Ministry of Health-funded LGBT groups launched the suicide prevention project lumi.be and a dedicated transgender youth suicide prevention site, gendervonk.be.

Discovering Belgium's 2024 guide lists current rights and where to report homophobia. Pride march demands have included gay relationships in high school sex education.

Between 2006 and 2014 there were 70 LGBT domestic adoptions recorded in Belgium: 58 male couples and 2 female couples in Flanders, plus 12 adoptions in the French Community.

Transgender journalist Bo Van Spilbeeck's coming-out in 2018 received widespread coverage, and homosexuality is widely accepted in media.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Federal Justice Department states that the 2017 procedure requires no medical conditions, while the Brussels-Capital Region's identity-card page still lists a medical certificate attesting to a sex change and possibly a judicial or administrative decision. Which requirement applies to a given application at a given commune is unresolved in the sources.

The status of replacement provisions following the Constitutional Court's partial annulment of 19 June 2019 is unresolved: the sources confirm only that applications continue under the current procedure pending new provisions.

The specific index score and per-category compliance figures on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map page are not carried in this inventory; only the page's existence as a formal-law snapshot is sourced here.

No source in the inventory gives enforcement outcomes, case counts or prosecution figures for transphobic hate crime specifically. The dating-app assault pattern is documented chiefly against gay men, and the incidence of equivalent attacks against trans people is not broken out.

Enforcement data for the 2023 conversion-practices ban, and for the 2023 femicide law, is not sourced here. The intersex position is likewise partly unresolved: nonconsensual surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, while one Brussels court judgment held a hospital accountable.

Whether the protections and procedures described apply unchanged to a short-term visitor presenting foreign documents is not addressed by any source in the inventory.
